title: Spanish for everyday moments
description: Build practical Spanish with 25 lessons across five units, from first greetings to everyday conversations.

unit.title: Your first conversations
unit.description: Say hello, order at a café, find your way, and get to know someone.

lessons.title: Your first hello
lessons.subtitle: Small words. New connections.

phrases.note: A friendly hello for any time of day.
Use this to greet someone in the morning.
Me llamo literally means ‘I call myself.’ Add your name.
A warm response when you meet someone new.
One little word that goes a long way.
An everyday way to say goodbye.

exercises.title: Start with a hello.
exercises.instruction: How do you say “Hello” in Spanish?
exercises.explanation: Hola means hello. The h is silent.

exercises.title: A brighter way to start the day.
exercises.instruction: What does “Buenos días” mean?
exercises.hint: You say this when you greet someone in the morning.
exercises.explanation: Buenos días means good morning. Días has an accent on the í.

exercises.title: Make an introduction.
exercises.instruction: Build this in Spanish: “Hello, my name is Alex.”
exercises.hint: Start with Hola, then me llamo, then the name.
exercises.explanation: Hola, me llamo Alex. Use me llamo before your name.

exercises.title: Lovely to meet you.
exercises.instruction: Someone introduces themselves. Say “Nice to meet you.”
exercises.hint: Mucho gusto is a friendly response to an introduction.
exercises.explanation: Mucho gusto means nice to meet you. You can use it with anyone you’re meeting for the first time.

exercises.title: Make a few connections.
exercises.instruction: Choose a Spanish phrase, then its English meaning.
exercises.hint: Hola → Hello · Gracias → Thank you · Buenos días → Good morning · Mucho gusto → Nice to meet you.
exercises.explanation: Four useful phrases, ready for your first conversation.

exercises.title: A little gratitude.
exercises.instruction: Write “Thank you” in Spanish.
exercises.hint: It starts with gra… The word is gracias.
exercises.explanation: Gracias. Simple, friendly, and always useful.

exercises.title: Until next time.
exercises.instruction: How do you say “See you later”?
exercises.hint: Hasta luego is an everyday goodbye.
exercises.explanation: Hasta luego means see you later. The h in hasta is silent, too.

exercises.title: Put a name to the greeting.
exercises.instruction: Build this in Spanish: “Nice to meet you, Ana.”
exercises.hint: The greeting is Mucho gusto. Put Ana at the end.
exercises.explanation: Mucho gusto, Ana. Add a name to make your greeting personal.

exercises.title: You know this one.
exercises.instruction: Write “Hello” in Spanish.
exercises.hint: Four letters, starting with a silent h: hola.
exercises.explanation: ¡Hola! You’ve got your first greeting.

exercises.title: Keep the conversation going.
exercises.instruction: Ana says “Hola, me llamo Ana.” Choose “Nice to meet you.”
exercises.hint: Respond to Ana’s introduction with Mucho gusto.
exercises.explanation: Hola, me llamo Ana. — Mucho gusto. That’s a real introduction, in Spanish.

exercises.title: Now it’s your turn.
exercises.instruction: Build this in Spanish: “Hello, my name is Sam.”
exercises.explanation: Hola, me llamo Sam. Same pattern, a different name.

exercises.title: Finish with a friendly goodbye.
exercises.instruction: Write “See you later” in Spanish.
exercises.explanation: ¡Hasta luego! You can say hello, introduce yourself, and say goodbye.

lessons.title: A stop at the café
lessons.subtitle: Order something. Make yourself at home.

phrases.note: Un is the masculine form of “a.” Café has a written accent on é.
Quisiera is a polite way to say what you would like.
Con means “with.” Use this after your order: un café con leche.
Sin means “without.” Azúcar has a written accent on ú.
Use cuesta for one thing. The question word cuánto has an accent.
La cuenta is the bill at a café or restaurant. Por favor makes the request polite.

exercises.title: Your first order.
exercises.instruction: Choose “A coffee, please.”
exercises.hint: Un café is a coffee. Add por favor to say please.
exercises.explanation: Un café, por favor. A short, polite way to order.

exercises.title: Something to drink.
exercises.instruction: What does “Quisiera agua” mean?
exercises.hint: Agua means water. Quisiera means I would like.
exercises.explanation: Quisiera agua means I would like water.

exercises.title: Put your order together.
exercises.instruction: Build “A coffee, please.”
exercises.explanation: Un café, por favor. In writing, café keeps its accent.

exercises.title: Make it your own.
exercises.instruction: Choose “With milk.”
exercises.hint: Con means with. Leche means milk.
exercises.explanation: Con leche. You can add it to an order: un café con leche.

exercises.title: Connect the café phrases.
exercises.instruction: Match each Spanish phrase to its English meaning.
exercises.hint: Con = with · Sin = without · Agua = water · La cuenta = the bill.
exercises.explanation: You can ask for a drink, say how you want it, and ask for the bill.

exercises.title: Skip the sugar.
exercises.instruction: Write “Without sugar” in Spanish.
exercises.hint: Sin + azúcar. Remember the accent on ú.
exercises.explanation: Sin azúcar. Sin is the opposite of con.

exercises.title: Hear a polite request.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the Spanish phrase you hear.
exercises.explanation: Quisiera agua. Quisiera is a useful polite request.
exercises.prompt: Write what you hear in Spanish.

exercises.title: Ready for the bill.
exercises.instruction: Build “The bill, please.”
exercises.hint: Start with La cuenta, then add por favor.
exercises.explanation: La cuenta, por favor. This asks for the bill, not the price of just one item.

exercises.title: Check the price.
exercises.instruction: What does “¿Cuánto cuesta?” mean?
exercises.hint: Cuánto asks how much. Cuesta means it costs.
exercises.explanation: ¿Cuánto cuesta? Ask this about one item.

exercises.title: Ask before you order.
exercises.instruction: Write “How much does it cost?” in Spanish.
exercises.hint: ¿Cuánto cuesta? Keep the accent on á.
exercises.explanation: ¿Cuánto cuesta? Spanish questions use an opening ¿ and a closing ?.

exercises.title: Listen at the counter.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the Spanish order you hear.
exercises.hint: You will hear Un café, por favor.
exercises.explanation: Un café, por favor. You have heard and built this order.
exercises.prompt: Write the order in Spanish.

exercises.title: Wrap up your café visit.
exercises.instruction: Write “The bill, please” in Spanish.
exercises.explanation: La cuenta, por favor. When you receive it, you can add Gracias.

lessons.title: Find your way
lessons.subtitle: A few words can take you somewhere new.

phrases.note: Use disculpa with one person in an informal situation. Disculpe is the formal alternative.
Dónde asks where. Use está to ask where one place is.
Derecha means right. A la derecha tells someone the direction.
Izquierda means left. Keep a la together before the direction.
Todo recto is a common direction, especially in Spain. Siga recto is a formal “go straight ahead.”
Cerca means near. Está cerca tells you the place is nearby.

exercises.title: Start politely.
exercises.instruction: Choose “Excuse me” to get someone’s attention.
exercises.hint: Disculpa is the informal way to get someone’s attention.
exercises.explanation: Disculpa. Use disculpe if you want to be more formal.

exercises.title: Find the station.
exercises.instruction: What does “¿Dónde está la estación?” mean?
exercises.hint: Dónde = where · la estación = the station.
exercises.explanation: ¿Dónde está la estación? One question can help you find a place.
options: How much does the ticket cost?

exercises.title: Build your question.
exercises.instruction: Build “Where is the station?”
exercises.explanation: ¿Dónde está la estación? Dónde, está, and estación each keep their written accent.

exercises.title: Pick a direction.
exercises.instruction: Choose “To the right.”
exercises.explanation: A la derecha means to the right. A la izquierda means to the left.

exercises.title: Read the directions.
exercises.instruction: Match each Spanish direction to its English meaning.
exercises.hint: Derecha = right · Izquierda = left · Recto = straight · Cerca = near.
exercises.explanation: These four phrases help you follow a short set of directions.

exercises.title: Take the other turn.
exercises.instruction: Write “To the left” in Spanish.
exercises.explanation: A la izquierda. Both left and right use a la in these direction phrases.

exercises.title: Hear the route.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the Spanish direction you hear.
exercises.explanation: Todo recto means straight ahead.
exercises.prompt: Write the direction in Spanish.

exercises.title: It is not far.
exercises.instruction: Build “It is nearby.”
exercises.explanation: Está cerca. Here está describes the location of a place.

exercises.title: Keep going ahead.
exercises.instruction: What does “Todo recto” mean in directions?
exercises.explanation: Todo recto tells you to continue straight ahead.

exercises.title: Ask for a moment.
exercises.instruction: Write “Excuse me” in Spanish to get someone’s attention.
exercises.hint: Use Disculpa informally or Disculpe formally.
exercises.explanation: Disculpa and disculpe both work. Choose the form that fits how you address the person.

exercises.title: Hear the next turn.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the Spanish direction you hear.
exercises.hint: You will hear A la derecha.
exercises.explanation: A la derecha. Listen for the whole phrase, not just derecha.
exercises.prompt: Write the direction in Spanish.

exercises.title: Ask the whole question.
exercises.instruction: Write “Where is the station?” in Spanish.
exercises.hint: ¿Dónde está la estación? Accents: ó, á, ó.
exercises.explanation: Disculpa, ¿dónde está la estación? You can now open politely and ask your question.

lessons.title: Get to know someone
lessons.subtitle: Go from a greeting to a conversation.

phrases.note: Use this with one person you address informally. ¿Cómo está usted? is a formal alternative.
Estoy describes how you feel right now. Bien means well.
De dónde asks “from where.” Eres means “you are” when addressing one person informally.
Use soy de before the place you are from. México keeps its written accent.
Hablo means I speak. Un poco de means a little of. Español uses ñ.
Use this to ask the same question back informally. Tú has an accent when it means “you.”

exercises.title: Beyond hello.
exercises.instruction: Choose “How are you?” when talking informally to one person.
exercises.explanation: ¿Cómo estás? This asks how the person is feeling.

exercises.title: Give a simple answer.
exercises.instruction: What does “Estoy bien” mean?
exercises.explanation: Estoy bien. You can add gracias: Estoy bien, gracias.

exercises.title: Answer with a thank-you.
exercises.instruction: Build “I am well, thank you.”
exercises.explanation: Estoy bien, gracias. Combine your new phrase with gracias from your first lesson.

exercises.title: Ask about home.
exercises.instruction: What does “¿De dónde eres?” mean?
exercises.explanation: ¿De dónde eres? This asks where someone is from, not where they are right now.

exercises.title: Keep the exchange going.
exercises.instruction: Match each Spanish phrase to its English meaning.
exercises.hint: Cómo = how · Soy de = I am from · Y tú = and you.
exercises.explanation: Answer a question, then ask ¿Y tú? to invite the other person to share.

exercises.title: Talk about where you are from.
exercises.instruction: Write “I am from Mexico” in Spanish.
exercises.hint: Soy de + México. Remember é in México.
exercises.explanation: Soy de México. Change México to the place you are from when you introduce yourself.

exercises.title: Give the question back.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the Spanish phrase you hear.
exercises.explanation: ¿Y tú? A short way to return a question. Keep the accent on tú.
exercises.prompt: Write the phrase in Spanish.

exercises.title: Say what you can speak.
exercises.instruction: Build “I speak a little Spanish.”
exercises.explanation: Hablo un poco de español. Un poco de tells someone you speak a little.

exercises.title: Name your new skill.
exercises.instruction: What does “Hablo un poco de español” mean?
exercises.hint: Hablo means I speak. Un poco means a little.
exercises.explanation: Hablo un poco de español. You can already use a little Spanish in real conversations.

exercises.title: Ask how someone is.
exercises.instruction: Write “How are you?” using the informal singular form.
exercises.hint: ¿Cómo estás? Both cómo and estás have accents.
exercises.explanation: ¿Cómo estás? This uses tú, the informal singular “you,” even though tú is not written.

exercises.title: Listen to a question.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the Spanish question you hear.
exercises.explanation: ¿De dónde eres? Dónde keeps its accent in questions.
exercises.prompt: Write the question in Spanish.

exercises.title: Make it a conversation.
exercises.instruction: Write “And you?” using the informal singular form.
exercises.explanation: Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? You can answer and keep the conversation going.

lessons.title: Your first day, in Spanish
lessons.subtitle: Put the whole unit into practice.

phrases.note: Combine hola with me llamo and a name. This is the introduction pattern from lesson 1.
Use soy for who you are or where you are from; estoy bien describes how you feel.

phrases.translation: I would like a coffee, please
phrases.note: Combine quisiera from the café lesson with un café and por favor.
acceptedAnswers: Me gustaría un café, por favor

phrases.note: Dónde está asks where one place is. La estación is the station.
Remember the contrast: derecha is right; izquierda is left.
Close a brief conversation with a thank-you and a friendly goodbye.

exercises.title: Meet someone at the café.
exercises.instruction: Choose “Hello, my name is Alex.”
exercises.explanation: Hola, me llamo Alex. Start with the introduction you learned in lesson 1.

exercises.title: Answer the next question.
exercises.instruction: Someone asks “¿De dónde eres?” Choose “I am from Mexico.”
exercises.explanation: Soy de México answers where you are from.

exercises.title: Place a polite order.
exercises.instruction: Build “I would like a coffee, please.”
exercises.explanation: Quisiera un café, por favor. You combined two patterns from the café lesson.

exercises.title: Your next stop.
exercises.instruction: Choose “Where is the station?”
exercises.explanation: ¿Dónde está la estación? You can start with Disculpa to get someone’s attention.

exercises.title: Bring the unit together.
exercises.instruction: Match each Spanish phrase to its English meaning.
exercises.hint: Me llamo = my name is · Soy de = I am from · Derecha = right · Hasta luego = see you later.
exercises.explanation: You can introduce yourself, say where you are from, follow a direction, and say goodbye.

exercises.title: Follow the directions.
exercises.instruction: Write “To the right” in Spanish.
exercises.explanation: A la derecha. The station is to the right in this practice conversation.

exercises.title: Hear an order.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the complete Spanish order you hear.
exercises.hint: You will hear Quisiera un café, por favor.
exercises.explanation: Quisiera un café, por favor. Notice the polite request at the start and por favor at the end.
exercises.prompt: Write the whole order in Spanish.

exercises.title: Leave on a friendly note.
exercises.instruction: Build “Thank you, see you later.”
exercises.explanation: Gracias, hasta luego. A friendly ending to a short exchange.

exercises.title: Recall your answer.
exercises.instruction: Write “I am from Mexico” in Spanish.
exercises.explanation: Soy de México. You recalled a phrase from the previous lesson.

exercises.title: Hear the question again.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the Spanish question you hear.
exercises.hint: You will hear ¿Dónde está la estación?
exercises.explanation: ¿Dónde está la estación? Listen for está, the form used for a place’s location.
exercises.prompt: Write the question in Spanish.

exercises.title: Introduce yourself from memory.
exercises.instruction: Write “Hello, my name is Alex” in Spanish.
exercises.explanation: Hola, me llamo Alex. You can replace Alex with your own name in real life.

exercises.title: Finish your first Spanish unit.
exercises.instruction: Write “Thank you, see you later” in Spanish.
exercises.explanation: Gracias, hasta luego. You completed greetings, a café visit, directions, small talk, and a full unit review.

lessons.title: Start with breakfast
lessons.subtitle: Say what you want, and what you need.

phrases.translation: What do you want to have for breakfast?
phrases.note: Desayunar means to have breakfast. Quieres is the informal singular form of “you want.”

phrases.translation: Do you want tea or coffee?
phrases.note: O means “or.” The accent distinguishes té, the drink, from te, a pronoun.
Quiero means I want. You already know con: it means with.
Y joins two things: huevos y pan. Huevos means eggs.
Use un before té, just as you used un café. Keep the accent on té.
Spanish uses tener, “to have,” for hunger. Put no before tengo to make it negative.
Tener sed literally means to have thirst. Tengo sed means I am thirsty.
When talking about food, está muy bueno says it tastes very good.

exercises.title: Understand the question.
exercises.instruction: What does “¿Qué quieres desayunar?” mean?
exercises.hint: It means: What do you want to have for breakfast?
exercises.explanation: Desayunar means to have breakfast. Quieres is the informal singular form of “you want.”
options: What do you want to have for breakfast?
exercises.answer: What do you want to have for breakfast?

exercises.title: Find the words you need.
exercises.instruction: Choose “Do you want tea or coffee?” in Spanish.
exercises.explanation: O means “or.” The accent distinguishes té, the drink, from te, a pronoun.

exercises.title: Put the phrase together.
exercises.instruction: Build this in Spanish: “I want bread with cheese”
exercises.explanation: Quiero means I want. You already know con: it means with.

exercises.title: Connect the meanings.
exercises.instruction: Match each Spanish phrase to its English meaning.
exercises.hint: Tengo sed → I am thirsty · No tengo hambre → I am not hungry · Un té, por favor → A tea, please · ¿Quieres té o café? → Do you want tea or coffee?
exercises.explanation: These phrases belong to the same situation. Recognize the whole meaning, then use the phrase in context.

exercises.title: Recall the reply.

exercises.title: Hear it once more.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the complete Spanish phrase you hear.
exercises.explanation: Tener sed literally means to have thirst. Tengo sed means I am thirsty.
exercises.prompt: Write the whole phrase in Spanish.

exercises.title: Use your voice.
exercises.instruction: Say this in Spanish: “I want bread with cheese”
exercises.explanation: Quiero means I want. You already know con: it means with.

exercises.title: Put it all together.
exercises.instruction: Build this in Spanish: “I am thirsty”
exercises.explanation: Tener sed literally means to have thirst. Tengo sed means I am thirsty.

exercises.title: Choose your drink.

exercises.explanation: Use un before té, just as you used un café. Keep the accent on té.

lessons.title: A meal out
lessons.subtitle: Read the menu, make a choice, and enjoy it.

phrases.translation: What would you like to eat?
phrases.note: Desea is a polite, formal way to ask what someone wants. Comer means to eat.

phrases.translation: Do you prefer meat or fish?
phrases.note: Prefiere is the formal singular form. Carne is meat; pescado is fish as food.

phrases.target: Una mesa para dos, por favor
phrases.note: Para can mean for. Una mesa is a table; dos is two.

phrases.translation: I would like the vegetable soup
phrases.note: Quisiera makes a polite request. Verduras means vegetables.
acceptedAnswers: Me gustaría la sopa de verduras

phrases.note: Prefiero means I prefer. Use it to say which option you want.
You learned sin azúcar at the café. The same sin pattern works with carne.
Puede is the formal singular form of “can you.” Traer means to bring.
Todo means everything here. Delicioso describes the food you are enjoying.

exercises.title: Understand the question.
exercises.instruction: What does “¿Qué desea comer?” mean?
exercises.hint: It means: What would you like to eat?
exercises.explanation: Desea is a polite, formal way to ask what someone wants. Comer means to eat.
options: What would you like to eat?

lessons.title: At the market
lessons.subtitle: Buy a little, buy a few, and know the price.

phrases.translation: How many apples would you like?
phrases.note: Cuántas asks how many with a feminine plural noun, such as manzanas.
Algo means something; más means more. Shopkeepers often shorten the question to ¿Algo más?

phrases.translation: How much does a kilo cost?
phrases.note: Use the price question from unit 1, adding un kilo for the amount.
Cuatro is four. Manzanas is the plural of manzana.
Nada means nothing. Nada más is a polite way to finish an order.

phrases.target: Medio kilo de tomates, por favor
phrases.translation: Half a kilo of tomatoes, please
phrases.note: Medio kilo means half a kilogram. Use de before what you are buying.
Tiene addresses one person formally. Fruta is feminine, so the adjective is fresca.
Use son, the plural form of “to be,” with amounts such as tres euros.

exercises.title: Understand the question.
exercises.instruction: What does “¿Cuántas manzanas quiere?” mean?
exercises.hint: It means: How many apples would you like?
exercises.explanation: Cuántas asks how many with a feminine plural noun, such as manzanas.
options: Half a kilo of tomatoes, please
How many apples would you like?

exercises.title: Find the words you need.
exercises.instruction: Choose “Anything else?” in Spanish.
exercises.explanation: Algo means something; más means more. Shopkeepers often shorten the question to ¿Algo más?

exercises.title: Put the phrase together.
exercises.instruction: Build this in Spanish: “How much does a kilo cost?”
exercises.explanation: Use the price question from unit 1, adding un kilo for the amount.

exercises.title: Connect the meanings.
exercises.instruction: Match each Spanish phrase to its English meaning.
exercises.hint: ¿Algo más? → Anything else? · Son tres euros → It is three euros · Nada más, gracias → Nothing else, thank you · ¿Tiene fruta fresca? → Do you have fresh fruit?
exercises.explanation: These phrases belong to the same situation. Recognize the whole meaning, then use the phrase in context.

exercises.title: Listen for the whole phrase.
exercises.instruction: Listen, then write the Spanish phrase you hear.
exercises.hint: You will hear: Medio kilo de tomates, por favor
exercises.explanation: Medio kilo means half a kilogram. Use de before what you are buying.
exercises.prompt: Write what you hear in Spanish.
